intent: Let a downstream context adopt an upstream context's model verbatim, with no translation, accepting the upstream's language as the cost of avoiding a translation layer.
problem: The upstream is outside your control — a vendor, a legacy system, or a context your architect has declared dominant — and building a translation layer costs more than it returns, while translating anyway leaves you with two vocabularies for one idea.
context: Conformist is one half of the customer-supplier pair; when the downstream has no negotiating power, the two options are to conform or to build an anti-corruption layer. Choose conformist when the upstream model is good enough, when it is an industry standard, or when the translation cost is genuinely prohibitive. Choose the ACL when the downstream is a core subdomain, when the upstream model is a mess you should not adopt, or when the upstream changes often enough that translation pays for itself. Conformist simplifies integration enormously — no translation, and one shared ubiquitous language across both teams.
benefits: Zero translation cost: the downstream model is the upstream model.
Both teams end up with the same ubiquitous language over that area.
Integration code disappears; there is no layer to maintain or re-translate.
Cheapest correct answer when the upstream model is an industry standard.
Removes an entire category of translation defect.
tradeoffs: The downstream loses its own model; upstream changes propagate straight into downstream code.
The downstream is stuck with upstream vocabulary, which can never be refactored away without coordination.
When the upstream model is poor, conformity propagates the poor model rather than containing it.
The downstream becomes unable to evolve independently and loses ownership of its concepts.
Cost asymmetry is permanent: the price is paid on every upstream change, not once.
quality_attributes_note: simplicity 9 and performance 8 because there is no layer. extensibility 3 and maintainability 6 because upstream change cost is unbounded and one-sided.

participants.responsibility: Supplies the model; it may be external, legacy, or strategically dominant.
participants.notes: Typically a vendor, a legacy system, or a context whose priorities override the downstream's.

participants.responsibility: Adopts the upstream model as its own; gives up independent evolution of those concepts.
participants.notes: No room to negotiate about upstream changes.

participants.responsibility: The upstream language, now also the downstream's.
participants.notes: The upside of conformism: one ubiquitous language instead of two.

use_cases: An internal downstream consuming a canonical Customer model owned by a platform team with no appetite for negotiation.
An industry-standard vocabulary (ISO 4217 currency codes, IANA time zones) used directly rather than translated.
A legacy system whose model is good enough that a translation layer would add nothing.
A downstream deliberately subordinate by architecture: Live Monitoring conforming to the Live Scoring context.
avoid_when: The downstream is a core subdomain — do not conform a core domain to a foreign mess.
The upstream model changes often: every change lands in your code with no buffer.
The upstream model is semantically wrong or structurally poor.
The downstream has any negotiating power at all — customer-supplier is strictly better.
pitfalls: Choosing conformism by default because it is easier today, then discovering the upstream is hostile.
Conforming to a legacy model "temporarily", with no plan or trigger to translate later.
Importing upstream SDK types directly into the domain, so the upstream vocabulary is everywhere.
Assuming conformity is symmetric — it is a downstream decision with an upstream consequence.
Failing to record the relationship on the context map, so nobody knows who is exposed to whose churn.

related_patterns_notes.anti-corruption-layer: The direct alternative: the ACL translates instead of adopting. Choose ACL over conformism whenever the upstream model is poor or volatile.
related_patterns_notes.customer-supplier: Conformist is the customer-supplier relationship with the negotiation removed — use it when the supplier will not negotiate.
related_patterns_notes.mapper: The mechanical translation between two models that conformity avoids entirely.

anti_patterns: Conformism to a legacy model that is actively hostile to the downstream domain.
Leaking upstream persistence or wire types through the downstream domain layer.
A conformance relationship with no recorded exit plan and no named trigger to revisit it.
Conforming in the core domain while assuming a translation layer exists elsewhere.
Letting upstream naming become downstream naming in every module, not just at the boundary.
design_principles: The conformist approach can simplify integration enormously, as no translation nor anti-corruption layers would be needed (Graca).
A conformist relationship indicates that the code in the downstream context is totally dependent on the upstream: if a breaking change happens upstream, the downstream must adapt.
Downstream has no room to negotiate about changes.
Typically the upstream is legacy code or an external service outside the development teams' control.
The three options when coordination fails: abandon the supplier (separate ways), take full responsibility for translation (ACL), or adopt the foreign model (conformist).
best_practices: Record the conformist relationship explicitly on the context map, with its upstream named.
Confine the upstream vocabulary to the boundary layer so the domain at least has a seam to replace later.
Define the exit trigger up front: what upstream change would make an ACL worth building.
Never conform a core subdomain to a foreign or legacy model.
Prefer an industry-standard vocabulary as the upstream when you have the choice — then conformity costs nothing.
